notes.summary: This chapter traces how nationalism grew in Europe from the French Revolution (1789) to the unification of Germany and Italy and the Balkan crisis before the First World War, covering liberalism, the conservative order after 1815, the revolutions of 1830 and 1848, romanticism and national symbols. CBSE tests it through fact-based and source-based MCQs, assertion-reason, chronology and matching items, and 3–5 mark answers on unification and the role of culture.
keyPoints: French Revolution (1789) built a collective identity through the ideas of la patrie and le citoyen, a new tricolour flag, the National Assembly, a centralised administration with uniform laws, abolition of internal customs duties, uniform weights and measures, and French as the common language.

Napoleonic Civil Code (1804): ended privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property; in conquered areas feudalism and serfdom were abolished and guild restrictions removed.

Liberalism (Latin 'liber' = free): individual freedom, equality before the law and government by consent; economically, freedom of markets. The Zollverein (1834, led by Prussia) abolished tariff barriers and reduced currencies from over thirty to two.

Treaty of Vienna (1815), hosted by Austrian Chancellor Duke Metternich: the Bourbon dynasty was restored in France, buffer states were set up around France, and the German Confederation of 39 states was left in place.

Revolutionaries and revolts: Giuseppe Mazzini (born Genoa, 1807) founded Young Italy in Marseilles and Young Europe in Berne; the July Revolution of 1830 brought Louis Philippe to power and Belgium broke away from the Netherlands; the Treaty of Constantinople (1832) recognised Greece as independent.

Romanticism used culture to build nationhood: Herder praised German folk culture (das volk), the Grimm brothers published folk tales in 1812, and Karol Kurpinski turned the polonaise and mazurka into Polish national symbols; after the failed 1831 rebellion, Polish was used in Church gatherings as a weapon of resistance.

1848: the Frankfurt Parliament (opened 18 May 1848 in the Church of St Paul, 831 elected representatives) offered the crown to Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia, who rejected it; women were admitted only as observers in the visitors' gallery.
Germany: Prussia under Chief Minister Otto von Bismarck won three wars over seven years (against Austria, Denmark and France); William I was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles in January 1871.

Italy: seven states, with only Sardinia-Piedmont ruled by an Italian princely house; Cavour's alliance with France helped defeat Austria in 1859; Garibaldi's Red Shirts took the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1860; Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy in 1861.

Britain: the Act of Union (1707) formed the United Kingdom of Great Britain, and Ireland was incorporated in 1801. Nations were shown as female allegories — Marianne (France) and Germania (Germany, crown of oak leaves = heroism). After 1871 the Balkans became the main source of nationalist tension.
traps: Confusing the Treaty of Vienna (1815, conservative restoration) with the proclamation at Versailles (1871, German Empire).
Mixing up personalities: Mazzini (Young Italy), Cavour (Chief Minister of Sardinia-Piedmont), Garibaldi (Red Shirts), Bismarck (Prussia), Metternich (Austria), Renan ('What is a Nation?').
Thinking the Frankfurt Parliament succeeded or gave women the vote — it failed, and women were only observers.
Assuming early-19th-century liberals wanted universal adult suffrage — most supported the vote only for property-owning men.
Reversing the French revolutions of 1830 and 1848: 1830 installed Louis Philippe as constitutional monarch; 1848 forced him out and a republic was proclaimed.
notes.examTip: Keep a one-line timeline in mind (1789, 1804, 1815, 1821–32, 1830, 1834, 1848, 1859–61, 1871) and place each event on it before answering chronology or assertion-reason questions.

questions.text: Which of the following was a provision of Napoleon's Civil Code of 1804?
options: It restored the feudal dues paid by peasants to landlords
It did away with privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property
It gave the right to vote to all adult men and women
It made the Pope the head of the French administration
questions.explanation:
The Civil Code of 1804, also called the Napoleonic Code, did away with all privileges based on birth.
It established equality before the law and secured the right to property.
In the regions he conquered, Napoleon also abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues, so the Code did not restore feudal dues.
It did not introduce voting rights for all adults.

questions.text: Which French philosopher, in a lecture titled 'What is a Nation?' delivered at the University of Sorbonne in 1882, argued that a nation is a large-scale solidarity and that its existence is a daily plebiscite?
options: Giuseppe Mazzini
Johann Gottfried Herder
Frederic Sorrieu
Ernst Renan
questions.explanation:
Ernst Renan, a French philosopher, gave the lecture 'What is a Nation?' at the University of Sorbonne in 1882.
He argued that a nation is not formed by a common language, race or religion, but is the culmination of a long past of endeavours and sacrifice.
He described a nation as a large-scale solidarity whose existence is a daily plebiscite.
Herder was a German philosopher of folk culture, Mazzini an Italian revolutionary and Sorrieu a French artist.

questions.text: The French revolutionaries introduced several measures to create a sense of collective identity among the French people. Which of the following was NOT one of these measures?
options: Spreading the ideas of la patrie (the fatherland) and le citoyen (the citizen)
Adopting a new tricolour flag in place of the former royal standard
Encouraging the use of regional dialects instead of the French spoken in Paris
Abolishing internal customs duties and adopting a uniform system of weights and measures
questions.explanation:
The revolutionaries promoted la patrie and le citoyen, adopted the tricolour, renamed the Estates General the National Assembly, set up a centralised administration with uniform laws, abolished internal customs duties and introduced uniform weights and measures.
Regional dialects were discouraged, and French as spoken and written in Paris became the common language of the nation.
So encouraging regional dialects was not one of their measures.

questions.text: For the new middle classes of early-19th-century Europe, what did liberalism stand for in the economic sphere?
options: Freedom of markets and the abolition of state-imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital
State ownership of all factories and land
Strong guild control over trade in towns
High customs duties between neighbouring states
questions.explanation:
The word liberalism comes from the Latin root liber, meaning free.
Politically, it stood for individual freedom, equality before the law and government by consent.
In the economic sphere, it stood for freedom of markets and the abolition of state-imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital.
The many customs barriers, currencies and systems of weights in the German states were exactly what liberals wanted removed.

questions.text: The Zollverein, a customs union formed in 1834 at the initiative of Prussia, is significant because it:
options: created a single German parliament at Frankfurt
united Austria and Prussia under one emperor
abolished tariff barriers and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two
granted voting rights to all adult men in the German states
questions.explanation:
In 1834 a customs union, the Zollverein, was formed at the initiative of Prussia and joined by most of the German states.
It abolished tariff barriers and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two.
Together with a growing railway network, this economic unity strengthened the wider demand for national unification.
The Frankfurt Parliament came later, in 1848.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): The Greek struggle for independence, which began in 1821, received wide support from educated elites in West Europe.
Reason (R): Poets and artists hailed Greece as the cradle of European civilisation and mobilised public opinion to support its struggle against the Ottoman Empire.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.explanation:
Greece had been part of the Ottoman Empire since the fifteenth century, and its struggle for independence began in 1821.
Greek nationalists were supported by Greeks living in exile and by many West Europeans who admired ancient Greek culture.
Poets and artists praised Greece as the cradle of European civilisation and mobilised public opinion; the English poet Lord Byron joined the struggle and died of fever in 1824.
Both statements are true and R explains A. The Treaty of Constantinople (1832) recognised Greece as an independent nation.

questions.text: Metternich once remarked, 'When France sneezes, the rest of Europe catches cold.' The July Revolution of 1830 in France is an example of this. What did the July Revolution do?
options: It proclaimed Louis Napoleon as Emperor of France
It overthrew the Bourbon kings and installed a constitutional monarchy with Louis Philippe at its head
It completed the unification of Germany
It restored the Bourbon dynasty after Napoleon's defeat
questions.explanation:
The Bourbon kings, who had been restored to power after 1815, were overthrown in July 1830 by liberal revolutionaries.
The revolutionaries installed a constitutional monarchy with Louis Philippe at its head.
The revolution sparked an uprising in Brussels that led to Belgium breaking away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands — the spread of unrest that Metternich's remark refers to.
The Bourbon restoration itself took place in 1815, after Napoleon's defeat.

questions.text: After its partition at the end of the 18th century by Russia, Prussia and Austria, Poland no longer existed as an independent territory, yet national feelings were kept alive through culture. How did the composer Karol Kurpinski contribute to this?
options: By collecting German folk tales with his brother
By painting the female allegory Marianne
By leading a volunteer army called the Red Shirts
By celebrating the national struggle through operas and music, turning folk dances like the polonaise and mazurka into nationalist symbols
questions.explanation:
After its partition, Poland had no independent state, and Russia tried to suppress Polish national feeling.
Karol Kurpinski celebrated the national struggle through his operas and music, turning folk dances like the polonaise and mazurka into nationalist symbols.
Language also became a weapon: after an armed rebellion against Russian rule was crushed in 1831, the clergy used Polish for Church gatherings and religious instruction.
The Grimm brothers (German folk tales), Marianne (France) and Garibaldi's Red Shirts (Italy) belong to other national movements.

questions.text:
Match the symbols used in 19th-century European nationalist allegories and paintings with their meanings:
P. Broken chains
Q. Crown of oak leaves
R. Olive branch around the sword
S. Rays of the rising sun
1. Willingness to make peace
2. Being freed
3. Heroism
4. Beginning of a new era
questions.explanation:
Broken chains stood for being freed (P–2).
The crown of oak leaves stood for heroism, as the German oak was a symbol of heroism (Q–3).
The olive branch around the sword showed willingness to make peace (R–1).
Rays of the rising sun marked the beginning of a new era (S–4).
So the correct match is P–2, Q–3, R–1, S–4.

questions.text: Before unification in the mid-19th century, Italy was divided into seven states. Which of them was ruled by an Italian princely house?
options: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies
Sardinia-Piedmont
The Papal States
Lombardy-Venetia
questions.explanation:
In the mid-19th century Italy was divided into seven states.
Only Sardinia-Piedmont was ruled by an Italian princely house.
The north was under the Austrian Habsburgs, the centre was ruled by the Pope, and the southern regions were under the Bourbon kings of Spain.
This is why Sardinia-Piedmont, under King Victor Emmanuel II and his Chief Minister Cavour, led the unification of Italy.

questions.text:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
I. The Frankfurt Parliament convened in the Church of St Paul
II. The Treaty of Vienna was signed
III. Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of united Italy
IV. The Zollverein was formed at the initiative of Prussia
options: IV, II, I, III
II, I, IV, III
II, IV, III, I
II, IV, I, III
questions.explanation:
Treaty of Vienna — 1815 (II).
Zollverein formed — 1834 (IV).
Frankfurt Parliament convened — May 1848 (I).
Victor Emmanuel II proclaimed king of united Italy — 1861 (III).
So the correct order is II, IV, I, III.
